citations.quote: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Input finite nonempty state and action sets, upper reward estimates $\widetilde r(s,a)$, empirical transition laws $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, nonnegative transition radii $b_p(s,a)$, a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and fixed orders of the states and actions for tie-breaking. For a vector $v\in\mathbb R^S$, write $\operatorname{span}(v)=\max_s v(s)-\min_s v(s)$ and let $\Delta(S)$ be the probability simplex on $S$. Initialize $u_0(s)=0$. At iteration $i\ge1$, compute
$$u_i(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[\widetilde r(s,a)+\max_{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le b_p(s,a)}q\cdot u_{i-1}\right].$$
For each state, record the first action in the fixed order attaining the outer maximum and a maximizing transition vector $q_i(\cdot\mid s)$; the inner maximum exists because each nonempty feasible subset of $\Delta(S)$ is compact. If $\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})<\varepsilon$, return the recorded stationary deterministic policy, maximizing transition vectors, the vector $u_{i-1}$ used in that backup, and the iteration index. A deterministic maximizing transition vector can be computed by moving up to $\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}$ probability mass from the lowest-valued states to a highest-valued state, with the fixed state order resolving equal values; stop moving mass when that state reaches probability one. This finite rule makes the returned quantities measurable functions of the estimates. Otherwise continue. The algorithm is a partial procedure unless a separate termination result is established.

derivations.claim: For a probability vector $p$ and $0<\alpha\le1$, the ball $Q=\{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-p\|_1\le2\alpha\}$ equals the set of $z+w$ with $0\le z\le p$, $\sum z=1-\alpha$, $w\ge0$, and $\sum w=\alpha$. Indeed, if $q\in Q$, the coordinatewise minimum $p\wedge q$ has mass $1-\|p-q\|_1/2\ge1-\alpha$; scaling that minimum down to mass $1-\alpha$ gives such $z\le q$, and $w=q-z$. (For $\alpha=1$, take $z=0$.) Conversely $p-z$ and $w$ are nonnegative of mass $\alpha$, so $\|z+w-p\|_1\le2\alpha$. Consequently the support function is $\alpha\max_j v(j)+H_p^\alpha(v)$, where $H_p^\alpha(v)=\max_{0\le z\le p,\,\sum z=1-\alpha}z\cdot v$. This equality includes radii at least $2$, for which $\alpha=1$ and the ball is the whole simplex.

Put $\alpha_{s,a}=\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}$. If $\eta<1$, step 1.1 writes $F(v)=\eta\max_j v(j)\mathbf1+(1-\eta)G(v)$, where $$G(v)(s)=\max_a\frac{\widetilde r(s,a)+(\alpha_{s,a}-\eta)\max_j v(j)+H_{\widehat P_{s,a}}^{\alpha_{s,a}}(v)}{1-\eta}.$$ The map $G$ is monotone in every coordinate. Each expression inside its maximum increases by $c$ on replacing $v$ by $v+c\mathbf1$, because its coefficient mass is $(\alpha_{s,a}-\eta)+(1-\alpha_{s,a})=1-\eta$. Thus $G(v+c\mathbf1)=G(v)+c\mathbf1$. If $m=\min(v-w)$ and $M=\max(v-w)$, monotonicity applied to $w+m\mathbf1\le v\le w+M\mathbf1$ implies $m\mathbf1\le G(v)-G(w)\le M\mathbf1$. The common scalar term in the expression for $F$ disappears from span, giving $\operatorname{span}(F(v)-F(w))\le(1-\eta)\operatorname{span}(v-w)$.

Apply step 2.1 repeatedly to $u_i=F(u_{i-1})$ and $u_{i-1}=F(u_{i-2})$. This proves the displayed geometric bound by induction. Its right side tends to zero, so the strict span test holds at some finite iteration for every positive tolerance. If $\eta=1$, every row ball is the whole simplex and $F(v)(s)=\max_a\widetilde r(s,a)+\max_jv(j)$; hence $F(v)-F(w)$ is constant across states and every increment after the first has zero span. UCRL2's logarithms, denominators, and tolerance at every finite $t_k\ge1$, $\delta\in(0,1)$ give positive radii and tolerance, so this applies to each episode without any confidence-event qualification.

derivations.claim: By [F2], each pair's observed samples are prefixes of a fixed i.i.d. tape with law $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$. By [F1], its reward coordinate has mean $r(s,a)$ and its next-state coordinate has law $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$. Rewards and indicators of next-state subsets lie in $[0,1]$. The finite tape construction uses AC exactly as stated in [A1].

By [F4] and [F5], the centered reward tape prefix has martingale partial sums with width-one increments; applying [F3] to that sum and to its negative gives the two-sided prefix tail $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. For a fixed pair and $n$, set $\varepsilon_r=\sqrt{7\log(4SAT/\delta)/(2n)}$. Step 1.1 bounds the failure probability by $2(\delta/(4SAT))^7$. Union over at most $SA$ pairs and $T$ possible prefix lengths gives at most $2SAT(\delta/(4SAT))^7\le\delta/2$.

For transition observations, fix a subset $B\subseteq S$. By step 1.1, the indicators $\mathbf1_{\{S'\in B\}}$ have mean $P(B\mid s,a)$ and range $[0,1]$. Their centered tape coordinates satisfy [F4]; by [F5] their partial sums are martingales, so [F3] gives $2e^{-2n u^2}$ for a deviation larger than $u$. For two probability vectors $p,q$ on a finite set, $\|p-q\|_1=2\max_{B\subseteq S}|p(B)-q(B)|$: the positive coordinates of $p-q$ sum to half its $\ell^1$ norm, and choosing exactly those coordinates attains the maximum. Therefore an $\ell^1$ deviation larger than $\varepsilon$ implies that some subset indicator deviates by more than $\varepsilon/2$. A union bound over the $2^S$ subsets gives $2^{S+1}e^{-n\varepsilon^2/2}$.

Set $L=\log(4AT/\delta)$ and $\varepsilon_p=\sqrt{14S L/n}$. Step 2.2 gives per-pair, per-prefix failure probability at most $2^{S+1}e^{-7SL}$. Union over at most $SAT$ pairs and prefixes is at most $SAT2^{S+1}e^{-7SL}\le\delta/2$: after dividing by $\delta/2$, its logarithm is $\log S+L+S\log2-7SL\le(2S)L-7SL\le0$, using $S\le2^{S-1}$ and $L\ge\log2$. Combining the reward failure bound from step 2.1 with the transition bound just obtained proves the simultaneous claim.

derivations.claim: Set $V_0(s)=0$ for every state. Finite-horizon backward induction attains each $V_n(s)$ because each action set is finite. For any $0\le j\le n$, splitting an $n$-step policy into its first $n-j$ and last $j$ rewards gives $V_n(y)\le V_{n-j}(y)+j$: the first part is at most the optimal $(n-j)$-step value and the last part is at most $j$ because rewards lie in $[0,1]$. For any $x,y$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F2] gives a policy from $x$ whose hitting time $\tau_y$ has expectation at most $D_0+\varepsilon$. Follow it until $y$ is hit, then use an optimal policy for the remaining $n-\tau_y$ steps if $\tau_y\le n$. On that event the total reward is at least $V_{n-\tau_y}(y)\ge V_n(y)-\tau_y$, since pre-hit rewards are nonnegative. On $\tau_y>n$, the total reward is nonnegative and $V_n(y)\le n<\tau_y$. Taking expectations and using [F8] gives $V_n(x)\ge V_n(y)-\mathbb E[\tau_y]\ge V_n(y)-D_0-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and interchanging $x,y$ proves $\max_s V_n(s)-\min_s V_n(s)\le D_0$.

Put $a_n=\max_s V_n(s)$; the maximum exists because $S$ is finite, and $0\le a_n\le n$ by [F1,F8]. For any $(m+n)$-step policy from $s$, the expected first $m$ rewards are at most $V_m(s)$, while conditional on the complete history through state $S_m$ the remaining $n$-step rule is an admissible policy from $S_m$ and its conditional expected reward is at most $V_n(S_m)\le a_n$. By [F4,F5,F6,F7], the unconditional expected total is therefore at most $V_m(s)+a_n\le a_m+a_n$, so $a_{m+n}\le a_m+a_n$. Conversely, choose $s_*$ attaining $a_m$ and use an optimal $m$-step policy from it; after observing $S_m=z$, continue with an optimal $n$-step policy from $z$. Input a finite communicating MDP, horizon $T\ge1$, confidence parameter $\delta\in(0,1)$, and fixed orders of states/actions. Start one episode at $t_1=1$. At the start $t_k$ of episode $k$, let $N_k(s,a)$ be the number of visits to $(s,a)$ before $t_k$, with empirical reward mean $\widehat r_k(s,a)=0$ and a fixed default probability vector when $N_k(s,a)=0$. Otherwise use the empirical mean reward and empirical next-state distribution. Put $n_k(s,a)=\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$ and
$$b^r_k(s,a)=\sqrt{\frac{7\log(2SAt_k/\delta)}{2n_k(s,a)}},\qquad b^p_k(s,a)=\sqrt{\frac{14S\log(2At_k/\delta)}{n_k(s,a)}}.$$
Set $\widetilde r_k(s,a)=\min\{1,\widehat r_k(s,a)+b^r_k(s,a)\}$. Run extended value iteration with these estimates/radii and tolerance $1/\sqrt{t_k}$, obtaining a stationary deterministic policy $\pi_k$. Let $v_k(s,a)$ start at zero and count visits within this episode. Follow $\pi_k$ until some $v_k(s,a)$ reaches $\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$, or until $T$ observations have been made; then start the next episode if time remains. All ties use the fixed orders. The positive radii ensure finite inner termination by the separate termination lemma. In particular, always $v_k(s,a)\le\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$; when $N_k(s,a)>0$, a completed triggering episode doubles that pair's total count.

Input finite nonempty state and action sets, upper reward estimates $\widetilde r(s,a)$, empirical transition laws $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, nonnegative transition radii $b_p(s,a)$, a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and fixed orders of the states and actions for tie-breaking. For a vector $v\in\mathbb R^S$, write $\operatorname{span}(v)=\max_s v(s)-\min_s v(s)$ and let $\Delta(S)$ be the probability simplex on $S$. Initialize $u_0(s)=0$. At iteration $i\ge1$, compute
$$u_i(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[\widetilde r(s,a)+\max_{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le b_p(s,a)}q\cdot u_{i-1}\right].$$
For each state, record the first action in the fixed order attaining the outer maximum and a maximizing transition vector $q_i(\cdot\mid s)$; the inner maximum exists because each nonempty feasible subset of $\Delta(S)$ is compact. If $\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})<\varepsilon$, return the recorded stationary deterministic policy, maximizing transition vectors, the vector $u_{i-1}$ used in that backup, and the iteration index. A deterministic maximizing transition vector can be computed by moving up to $\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}$ probability mass from the lowest-valued states to a highest-valued state, with the fixed state order resolving equal values; stop moving mass when that state reaches probability one. This finite rule makes the returned quantities measurable functions of the estimates. Otherwise continue. The algorithm is a partial procedure unless a separate termination result is established.

For every finite nonempty state/action system, bounded real upper rewards, probability-vector empirical centers, strictly positive transition radii, and tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, extended value iteration terminates. More precisely, write $F$ for its optimistic Bellman operator, put $\eta=\min_{s,a}\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}>0$, and set $u_0=0$, $u_i=F(u_{i-1})$. Then
$$\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})\le(1-\eta)^{i-1}\operatorname{span}(u_1),\qquad i\ge1.$$
When $\eta=1$, the span is zero for $i\ge2$. In particular, the positive UCRL2 confidence radii give finite stopping with tolerance $1/\sqrt{t_k}$ in every episode of a finite communicating MDP, including episodes whose confidence set misses the true model.

For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\max_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.

For a finite communicating MDP, let $\rho^*$ denote the common optimal average reward. The existence and independence of this value from the initial state are proved in the immediately cited theorem. Under any policy, write $R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\rho_t$ for the realized cumulative reward over the first $T$ interactions. The pathwise regret is the random variable $\Delta_T=T\rho^*-R_T$. Its expected regret is $\mathbb E[\Delta_T]=T\rho^*-\mathbb E[R_T]$. The pathwise random variable and its expectation are distinct objects.

Fix a finite-horizon interaction of length $T$ in a finite MDP with bounded rewards and any nonanticipating policy: each action distribution is a measurable function of the revealed history, and policy randomization is independent of unexposed MDP samples. On an enlarged probability space with the same law for the observed interaction, for each admissible pair $(s,a)$ there is a sequence $Z_{s,a,1},\ldots,Z_{s,a,T}$ of independent samples with common law $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ such that the $j$th observed next-state/reward pair at $(s,a)$ is $Z_{s,a,j}$ whenever that visit occurs.

Assume AC. Let $(M_k,\mathcal F_k)_{k=0}^n$ be a martingale. Suppose finite $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable $A_k,B_k$ and deterministic $c_k\ge0$ satisfy
$$A_k\le M_k-M_{k-1}\le B_k,\qquad B_k-A_k\le c_k$$
almost surely. Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2}\right),$$
and the analogous lower-tail bound holds, with the zero-denominator expression interpreted as $0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix $T\ge2$. At any integer time $t\ge1$, use [F4] to apply [F5] to every fixed pair and prefix length $1\le n<t$. Rewards give two-sided probability $2e^{-2nu^2}$; subset indicators give the same bound. For probability vectors $p,q$, $\|p-q\|_1=2\max_{B\subseteq S}|p(B)-q(B)|$, by summing positive coordinates of $p-q$. Union over $2^S$ subsets therefore bounds an $\ell^1$ error exceeding $u$ by $2^{S+1}e^{-nu^2/2}$. Substituting the algorithm's radii, and unioning over at most $SAt$ pairs and prefixes, bounds reward failure at time $t$ by $2SAt(\delta/(2SAt))^7\le\delta/(64t^6)$, and transition failure by $SAt2^{S+1}(\delta/(2At))^{7S}\le\delta/(32t^6)$. The latter follows from $S2^{1-6S}\le1/32$, whose value at $S=1$ is $1/32$ and whose successive ratio is $(S+1)/(64S)<1$. Unobserved-pair reward radii exceed $1$ and transition radii exceed $2$, so their defaults cannot fail. Since $\sum_{t\ge1}t^{-6}\le1+\int_1^\infty x^{-6}dx=6/5$, with probability at least $1-\delta/8$ every confidence set at every time contains the true transition/reward means. Denote this event by $E$. There is no conditioning on an adaptively selected count in this argument.

In an episode whose confidence set contains the true model, let $F$ be its optimistic Bellman operator. Its iterates $U_n=F^n0$ are optimal $n$-step values for the extended transition choices and fixed upper rewards, by finite-horizon backward induction and attained maxima. Upper rewards are in $[0,1]$, and true transitions and rewards are dominated admissible choices. Thus $U_n\ge V_n$. Also $\operatorname{span}(U_n)\le D$: from $x$, follow a true-model policy hitting $y$ in expected time at most $D+\xi$, and then an optimal remaining-horizon extended policy. The inequality $U_n(y)\le U_{n-j}(y)+j$ follows by dropping the last $j$ rewards, each at most one. For hitting time $\tau$, this yields total expected reward at least $U_n(y)-\mathbb E\tau$, including $\tau>n$ because $U_n(y)\le n$ and rewards are nonnegative. Take $\xi\downarrow0$ and interchange $x,y$. A true history policy's state/action path law can be realized in the extended system by its conditional action probabilities given state/action history; finite histories have finite state/action alphabets, so this averaging preserves its state transitions and hitting-time law.

Let $h_k$ be the vector used in the terminating backup, and let $d_k=F(h_k)-h_k$, with extrema $m_k,M_k$. By [F2], $M_k-m_k<\varepsilon_k=1/\sqrt{t_k}$. Monotonicity and additive homogeneity give $F^nh_k\le h_k+nM_k\mathbf1$. Also $F$ is sup-norm nonexpansive, since $v\le w+c\mathbf1$ implies $Fv\le Fw+c\mathbf1$ and conversely. Therefore $U_n\le h_k+nM_k\mathbf1+\|h_k\|_\infty\mathbf1$. Combine with $U_n\ge V_n$ and [F3], divide by $n$, and pass to the limit to get $\rho^*\le M_k$. Consequently $d_k(s)\ge\rho^*-\varepsilon_k$. For the chosen action and row, $d_k(s)=\widetilde r_k(s,a)+q_k(\cdot\mid s,a)h_k-h_k(s)$. On a good episode, $\widetilde r_k-r\le2b^r_k$ and $\|q_k-P\|_1\le2b^p_k$; step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{span}(h_k)\le D$. Centering $h_k$ halfway between its extrema bounds its sup norm by $D/2$, so $(q_k-P)h_k\le Db^p_k$. Hence each step of that episode obeys $\rho^*-r(s,a)\le (Ph_k)(s,a)-h_k(s)+Db^p_k(s,a)+2b^r_k(s,a)+\varepsilon_k$.

Subtract $\min h_k$ from each episode vector. On good episodes it lies in $[0,D]$. For the probabilistic argument define $w_k$ to be that vector when the episode's confidence set contains the true means and zero otherwise. This is measurable at the episode start, since true means are fixed parameters; its coordinates always lie in $[0,D]$. The increments $X_t=(Pw_{k(t)})(S_t,A_t)-w_{k(t)}(S_{t+1})$ are conditionally centered with conditional range width at most $D$. The reward differences $Y_t=r(S_t,A_t)-\rho_t$ are conditionally centered with width at most $1$, even if reward and next state are correlated. Apply [F5] separately with failure probability $\delta/4$ to obtain $\sum_{t\le T}X_t\le D\sqrt{(T/2)\log(4/\delta)}$ and $\sum_{t\le T}Y_t\le\sqrt{(T/2)\log(4/\delta)}$. These events and $E$ jointly have probability at least $1-\delta$, by step 1.1 and a union bound. On their intersection every episode is good; the sum of $(Ph_k)(S_t,A_t)-h_k(S_t)$ equals $\sum X_t$ plus episode endpoint differences, each at most $D$.

Write $K=\sum_s|A(s)|\le SA$ and $Q_T=\sum_{k,s,a}v_k(s,a)/\sqrt{\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}}$. For a fixed visited pair, the first observation contributes one. Thereafter, for $N\ge1$ and $0\le v\le N$, rationalization gives $v/\sqrt N=(\sqrt{N+v}-\sqrt N)(\sqrt{1+v/N}+1)\le(1+\sqrt2)(\sqrt{N+v}-\sqrt N)$. Telescoping, including the first observation, and then Cauchy--Schwarz yield $Q_T\le(1+\sqrt2)\sum_{s,a}\sqrt{N_T(s,a)}\le(1+\sqrt2)\sqrt{SAT}$. A completed episode can be charged to a triggering pair. A pair with final count $N$ receives at most $1+\log_2\max\{1,N\}$ charges, because after its initial observation every charge doubles its total. The last incomplete episode adds at most one. Thus concavity of $\log$ gives $m\le1+K+K\log_2(1+T/K)$. When $T\ge K$, this is at most $K(3+\log_2(T/K))\le4\sqrt{KT}\le4\sqrt{SAT}$. For the last inequality set $x=T/K\ge1$: $4\sqrt x-3-\log_2x$ is positive at $1$ and has derivative $(2\sqrt x-1/\log2)/x>0$, since $\log2>1/2$.

On the joint event of step 4.1, sum step 3.1 and use $\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}\le t_k\le T$. With $L_r=\log(2SAT/\delta)$ and $L_p=\log(2AT/\delta)$ this gives the fully explicit bound $$\Delta_T\le\left[D\sqrt{14S L_p}+\sqrt{14L_r}+1\right]Q_T+Dm+(D+1)\sqrt{\frac T2\log(4/\delta)}.$$ The $1$ in the bracket bounds the planning error $\sum_k\ell_k/\sqrt{t_k}$ by $Q_T$. This argument bounds realized regret; it does not replace rewards by their expectation without the martingale term.

Put $L=\log(T/\delta)$ and $B=DS\sqrt{ATL}$. If $T<SA$, then $\Delta_T\le T\le\sqrt{SAT}<34B$, since $D\ge1$ and $L\ge\log2>1/2$. Suppose $T\ge SA$ and $S\ge2$. Then $L_r\le3L$, $L_p\le2L$ (because $2A\le SA\le T$), and $\log(4/\delta)\le2L$. Divide step 6.1 by $B$ and apply step 5.1, $D\ge1$, and $A\ge1$ to bound the resulting coefficient by $$(1+\sqrt2)\left[\sqrt{28}+\sqrt{42/S}+\frac1{\sqrt{SL}}\right]+\frac4{\sqrt{SL}}+\frac2{S\sqrt A}<\frac52\left(\frac{16}3+\frac{14}3+1\right)+4+1=\frac{65}2<34.$$ Here $S\ge2$, $L>1/2$, $\sqrt{28}<16/3$, $\sqrt{21}<14/3$, and $1+\sqrt2<5/2$ justify each numerical bound.

If $S=1$, every Bellman vector is constant, so the transition term and episode endpoint terms vanish identically. With $A\le T$, $L_r\le3L$, and $\log(4/\delta)\le2L$, steps 5.1--6.1 give $\Delta_T/B\le(1+\sqrt2)(\sqrt{42}+1/\sqrt L)+1<\frac52(\frac{13}2+\frac32)+1=21<34$. The case $A>T$ was already covered in step 7.1. This completes the first assertion for every fixed $T\ge2$. Enlarging its logarithm gives the second assertion for those horizons. At $T=1$, $\Delta_1\le1$, whereas $34DS\sqrt{A\log(2/\delta)}>1$, proving the second assertion at the remaining boundary with probability one.

Consider one state $s$, two actions ordered $a_1<a_2$, deterministic self-transitions, and deterministic rewards $0$ for $a_1$ and $1$ for $a_2$. This is communicating with $S=1$, $A=2$, and $D=1$ by [F3]. At $T=1$ no pair has been observed before planning; both reward estimates are $0$, both transition laws are the same point mass, and the confidence bonuses coincide. Every EVI backup therefore ties the actions, so [F1] selects $a_1$. The optimal average reward is $\rho^*=1$, while $R_1=0$, hence $\Delta_1=1$ by [F3].

Set $\delta=e^{-1/100000}$. The proposed right side is $34\sqrt{2/100000}=34/\sqrt{50000}<1$, since $34^2=1156<50000$. Thus the event asserted in the Statement has probability $0$, whereas its required probability is $1-\delta>0$. This contradicts the claim for the permitted horizon $T=1$.

Assume AC. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one measurable space, with
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
the event-supremum convention without a factor $1/2$,
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le\sqrt{\frac12D(P\|Q)}.$$
If $P\not\ll Q$, the right side is $+\infty$ by the definition of KL
divergence.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $|f|\le M$ pointwise for some finite $M\ge0$. With the convention
$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
one has
$$\left|\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ\right|\le 2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$
For every measurable $g:E\to\mathbb R$ with $0\le g\le M$ pointwise, one also has
$$\left|\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ\right|\le M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$
Both integral differences are zero when $M=0$.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

derivations.claim: We use the proved local Pinsker inequality and the total-variation bound for expectations. All remaining probability calculations are supplied here. Write $\operatorname{kl}(p,q)$ for Bernoulli relative entropy. For $0<p<p+e<1$, $$\operatorname{kl}(p,p+e)=\int_p^{p+e}\frac{x-p}{x(1-x)}\,dx\le\frac{e^2}{2p(1-p-e)}.$$ Indeed, differentiating $p\log(p/x)+(1-p)\log((1-p)/(1-x))$ gives the integrand, and $x(1-x)\ge p(1-p-e)$ on the integration interval. Suppose two environments differ only at a single state-action pair $j$, at which one Bernoulli observation parameter changes from $p$ to $p+e$. Let $P_0$ and $P_j$ be their complete histories through the $T$th transition/reward, and let $N_j$ count uses of pair $j$. Their likelihood ratio is the product of the changed Bernoulli likelihood ratios at those uses. The initial law and all conditional action kernels are identical and cancel, including for randomized algorithms. Taking logarithms, conditioning on each past history and selected action, and summing gives exactly $$\operatorname{KL}(P_0\Vert P_j)=\mathbb E_0[N_j]\operatorname{kl}(p,p+e).$$ There is no absolute-continuity issue because both Bernoulli parameters lie strictly between zero and one and every unchanged kernel has the same support. The displayed identity also follows directly by expanding the finite history probabilities; all rewards used below have finite support. citations.quote: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

derivations.claim: Starting from either state, the chain remains there at every time. From state $0$ every cumulative reward is $0$, so its average is $0$; from state $1$ every cumulative reward over $T$ steps is $T$, so its average is $1$.

No policy can leave either absorbing state. In particular, starting from $0$ there is no policy that reaches $1$ with finite expected hitting time, so the communicating condition fails. The distinct averages show why the theorem's communication hypothesis matters.

For a finite communicating MDP with rewards in $[0,1]$, let $V_n(s)$ be the supremum of the expected sum of the first $n$ rewards over all history-dependent policies starting from state $s$.
